unit: Students can describe their daily study routines, discuss learning tools, and share advice for building good study habits while balancing school and family life.
objective: Talk about how often you do different study activities.

title: Warm-up
subtitle: Daily routines and taking breaks
question: How do you organize your schedule to make time for breaks?
starters: Having a good schedule helps me...

title: Useful language (Part 1)
teacher_instructions: Read each word aloud and ask the student to repeat.
Read the definition and example sentence.
Ask the check question to confirm understanding.
Ask the student to make their own sentence using one of the words.

words.definition: Before the usual or expected time.
words.example: I wake up early to study before school.
words.check: What do you usually do early in the morning?

words.definition: After the usual or expected time.
words.example: He went to bed late because he had a lot of homework.
words.check: Is it better to study early in the morning or late at night?

title: Useful Language (Part 2)
teacher_instructions: Read each word aloud and ask the student to repeat it.
Read the definition and example sentence for each word.
Ask the check questions to confirm understanding.
Ask the student to make a sentence using one of the words.

words.definition: Not late; happening at the correct time.
words.example: I always finish my homework on time.
words.check: Which of these means you are on time: arriving at 8:00 for an 8:00 class, or arriving at 8:15?

words.definition: A plan of what you will do and when you will do it.
words.example: I have a busy study schedule this week.
words.check: Do you prefer to keep your schedule in a notebook or on your phone?

words.definition: A chart that shows the days, weeks, and months of the year.
words.example: I mark my test dates on my calendar.
words.check: What do you usually see on a calendar: months and days, or names and phone numbers?

title: Conversation Builder
goal: Discuss how often you do things in your schedule.

linkers.use: To talk about something you do every day or all the time.
To talk about something you do occasionally, but not every day.
To talk about something you almost never do.

model:
Tutor: So, do you look at your calendar every day?
Student: Yes, I always look at my calendar. I like to be on time.
Tutor: That's good. Do you ever study late at night?
Student: No, I rarely study late. I sometimes study early in the morning instead.

your_turn.teacher: Ask the student: Do you study late? Do you take breaks on time?
your_turn.student: Answer your tutor using 'I always', 'I sometimes', and 'I rarely'.

title: Let's practice
teacher_question: Let's talk about creating a good schedule so you have time for breaks. Imagine I'm your friend and I say: 'You know, I study really late every night. I never take breaks.' Disagree with me and tell me about your weekly schedule. Use the sentences below to help you.
student_guide: Actually, I rarely study _____ because I need time to rest.
I always check my _____ so I can finish my work on time.
Well, I sometimes wake up _____, but I make sure to take breaks.

title: Real-world scenario
role_a: Student: You are planning your weekly school schedule.
role_b: Tutor: You are helping the student plan their schedule. Suggest studying very late at night.
problem: You want to create a balanced schedule so you have time to take breaks, but your tutor wants you to study very late at night.
mission: Use the words always, sometimes, rarely, early, and late.
start: Alright, let's look at your calendar. I think we should plan to study very late every night. What do you think?

title: Wrap-up
recap: Vocabulary: early, late, on time, schedule, calendar
Language chunks: I always... / I sometimes... / I rarely...
Skill: Talk about how often you do study activities.
final_task: Use one of today's language chunks to tell me: What is one thing you do to keep a good study schedule?
challenge: Review your weekly calendar and practice saying three things you always do on time.
